articles.title: Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer highlights growing number of nonsmokers diagnosed with the disease – and younger people too
articles.author: Estelamari Rodriguez, Associate Director of Community Outreach in Thoracic Oncology, University of Miami
paras: When many people think of an average lung cancer patient, they often imagine an older man smoking. But the face of lung cancer has changed. Over the past 15 years, more women, never smokers and younger people are being diagnosed with lung cancer.

In fact, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death among women, and more women die from lung cancer than breast, ovarian and colorectal cancer each year. The American Lung Association reports that while lung cancer rates have risen by 79% for women over the last 44 years, they decreased by 43% for men. And for the first time in history, there are more young women than men diagnosed with lung cancer.

News about Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer diagnosis on Oct. 13, 2026, sparked discussion about increasing rates of the disease among people who have never smoked. Leo reportedly is not a smoker. Potential causes for the disease include environmental exposures and genetics, and recognizing the diverse factors that can increase someone’s risk of lung cancer – regardless of their smoking history – is essential for timely and appropriate screening and treatment.

Cancer that is found at the earliest stages, like that of the pope, can be treated with surgery and cured for both smokers and nonsmokers. The challenge is that people who have never smoked are not currently included in lung cancer screening guidelines, and tumors are often only found by chance.

As a thoracic oncologist, I have seen many younger women and never smokers walk into my clinic with a new diagnosis of lung cancer. Particularly for never smokers, lung cancer is unexpected for both patients and their doctors, which can often lead to delays in diagnosis. Researchers have described this trend of increasing lung cancer rates among women in different parts of the world and are starting to understand why cases are on the rise.
The first explanation of why rates of lung cancer in women have increased is that many started smoking later than men, pushing back their peak in smoking-related lung cancer diagnoses.

Women also started smoking in the years when filtered cigarettes were most commonly used. This led to an increased risk of a type of cancer called adenocarcinoma due to the way cigarette filters distribute tobacco smoke to the outer parts of the lungs. Some studies suggest that women are more susceptible to the carcinogenic effects of exposure to tobacco and cigarette smoke, including second-hand smoke, and may develop lung cancer after fewer years of smoking compared to men.

However, it is important to note that most people diagnosed today with lung cancer are not active smokers. About 20% of women with lung cancer have never smoked – higher than for men with lung cancer who’ve never smoked.
Besides smoking and secondhand smoke, there are several other lung cancer risk factors. These include a family history of cancer and exposure to asbestos, radon and air pollution.

Exposure to carcinogens in the workplace in the form of inhaled chemicals such as arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, silica and nickel is still a concern in some parts of the world. The potential lung cancer risk of e-cigarette and marijuana smoke is still under study but of potential concern.

Recently, researchers have also found that genetics can play a role in lung cancer risk in some patients with a strong history of lung cancer. Studies of these families have helped identify potential susceptibility genes for lung cancer and environmental risk factors.

Like BRCA1 and BRCA2 in breast cancer, alterations in genes that promote or protect against tumor development can contribute to lung cancer development. Researchers have yet to identify specific mutations that may predispose individuals to lung cancer. However, studying familial genetic predispositions can help elucidate how lung cancer develops and lead to new biomarkers for early cancer detection in high-risk groups.

In 2021, the United States Preventive Services Task Force updated its lung cancer screening guidelines to include younger patients with less smoking history. Now, lung cancer screening is recommended for adults ages 50 to 80 who have smoked at least one pack per day for 20 years, current smokers and former smokers who quit smoking within the last 15 years. Women at risk for lung cancer can talk to their doctors about ordering a low-dose CT scan for lung cancer screening.

Nationwide, more than 70% of eligible women undergo breast cancer screening but less than 6% of all eligible smokers pursue lung cancer screening. Researchers estimate that these new screening guidelines will increase the number of women eligible for lung cancer screening by 40% by including those at a younger age who have less smoking exposure.

In recent years, increasing understanding of the genetic changes that can lead to cancer and how to harness the immune system to treat cancer has led to new targeted therapies and immunotherapies that have improved the prognosis of patients with lung cancer. Women tend to have a better lung cancer prognosis than men, especially if they never smoked and have tumors with molecular changes that can be treated with targeted therapies.

However, lung cancer symptoms may go unrecognized in women. Symptoms of lung cancer can include coughing, shortness of breath, overwhelming fatigue and pain in the back, chest or shoulder, which could be confused for other ailments. Because women tend to be slightly younger when diagnosed than men, patients may be able to tolerate symptoms longer and delay seeking medical attention. Physicians also might not attribute these symptoms to lung cancer due to a patient’s younger age.

Recognizing the early symptoms of lung cancer, expanding lung cancer screening eligibility and testing for genetic biomarkers to select the best therapy are some of the steps that could help address the global epidemic of lung cancer in women.
This is an updated version of an article published on Feb. 1, 2023.
Estelamari Rodriguez is affiliated with University of Miami Health System. She receives funding from the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: Doing a short cardio session after weight training probably won’t boost your gains – here’s why
articles.author: Liam T. Pearson-Noseworthy, Distinguished Teaching Fellow, School of Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation, Northumbria University, Newcastle
paras: Spend long enough on fitness social media and you’ll see the same tip. Finish every weight training session with about 15 minutes of cardio to boost your “gains”. But does it actually work? Probably not as much as you’d think.
Doing cardio and weight training in the same exercise programme is known as “concurrent training”. This includes doing cardio in the same session as your weights, or on separate days.

For years, people thought concurrent training held back strength and muscle gains. This worry goes back to 1980 when a ten-week study found that people who did both on the same days, within two hours of each other, built less strength than those who only lifted.

This became known as the “interference effect”: the idea that cardio gets in the way of building muscle and strength. And there’s some logic to keeping cardio short. A 2012 review found that the longer and more often people did cardio alongside their lifting, the more it ate into their strength, muscle and power gains. That puts a 15-minute bout at the low-risk end.
But research has come a long way since 1980, and now shows the interference effect may not be as significant as once thought.
A major 2022 review pooled 43 studies involving 1,090 people. It compared people who did cardio alongside a weights programme against people who only did the weights programme.
Adding cardio made no real difference to how much muscle people built or how much stronger they got. That held whether the cardio was cycling or running.
A 2026 review of 17 earlier analyses covering 144 studies reached the same conclusion. It also found that adding cardio improved aerobic fitness without costing strength, power or muscle.

This research clearly shows that a cardio finisher isn’t going to wreck progress. But it’s also worth noting that this research didn’t suggest adding cardio made muscle or strength gains any bigger. On average, people who did cardio and weights gained similar muscle and strength to those who only lifted, though there are two exceptions to this finding.

The first is explosive strength, the kind you use to jump or sprint. This improved slightly less when people added cardio. But that dip only showed up when cardio and weights were done within 20 minutes of each other. When the two were at least three hours apart, it wasn’t there. A finisher done straight after lifting falls inside that window.

The second is experience. Across 27 studies, adding cardio held back leg strength gains in experienced gym-goers – but only when both were done in the same session. Beginners saw no clear difference. The 2026 review points out that there’s very little research on elite athletes, though, and they’re the people most likely to notice even a small dip in performance.
There’s also an early hint that adding cardio could affect the muscle fibres themselves. These are the individual cells that make up a muscle.

A review of 15 studies found that adding cardio to a weights programme may slightly reduce muscle fibre growth. This effect may be more pronounced with running than cycling – at least in one type of muscle fibre. But the authors were careful to call this research preliminary, and it didn’t show up when whole muscles were measured.

If you’re doing both weight training and cardio in one session, lift first. A review from Northumbria University found lifting before cardio provided about 7% greater gains in lower-body strength than the other way round.
A second review found the same pattern. But when it came to aerobic fitness, neither review found the order made any difference.
However, I couldn’t find any studies testing a 15-minute finisher head-on against separate cardio sessions. And the studies that are out there, on average, were judged to be of medium quality.

It’s also worth doing the maths: three 15-minute finishers a week adds up to 45 minutes. The UK’s chief medical officers recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus strength work on at least two days.

That gap matters. High aerobic fitness is linked to about half the risk of early death compared with low fitness. Doing both strength and aerobic exercise is linked to a 40% lower risk of early death than doing neither.
How much you do matters too. Even 75 minutes of moderate activity a week is linked to a 23% lower risk of early death compared with doing none – with the biggest gains up to around 150 minutes.
What about fat loss, the other big selling point of the cardio finisher?

A 2025 review of 36 studies found that people who added cardio to their weight training programme lost about 1kg more fat than those who only lifted – but only in studies lasting ten weeks or more. That gap also disappeared in studies where both groups trained for the same length of time or burned roughly the same calories. Same-day or separate-day cardio made no difference.

The bottom line is that if you enjoy doing your cardio after a weight training session, then you should keep doing it. A short finisher won’t hurt your gains, and it works your heart and lungs in ways you might not otherwise with weight training alone.

If muscle size is your main goal, a bike may be a slightly safer bet than a treadmill. Running, but not cycling, has been linked to smaller gains in muscle size and strength – though the evidence is still thin.

If power is your priority, or you’re an experienced lifter chasing a personal best, give cardio its own session a few hours later if possible. Just don’t treat a finisher as a shortcut to bigger or stronger “gains”, or as your cardio done for the week. It’s a good start, not the whole job.

articles.title: A drug can make children with the most common form of dwarfism taller – but height isn’t the same as a better life
articles.author: Erin Pritchard, Senior lecturer in Disability Studies, Liverpool Hope University
paras: A drug that helps children with the most common form of dwarfism grow taller has sparked an ethical debate within the dwarfism community.

Some parents hope that as well as increasing size, it will prevent serious health complications and improve their children’s independence. But critics worry that a treatment focused on increasing height sends the message that dwarfism is something that needs to be corrected.

The drug, vosoritide, sold as Voxzogo, is used to treat children with achondroplasia, a genetic condition that restricts bone growth. It works by reducing the activity of a signal that slows bone growth. Approved in Europe in 2021, it is now authorised for children from four months old while their bones are still growing.
Clinical trials show that vosoritide increases growth. But whether it can prevent serious medical complications or improve quality of life in the longer term remains uncertain.
This raises difficult questions about what constitutes a successful treatment and how much say people with achondroplasia should have in deciding what those outcomes should be.
Growth rate measures bones, not lives

The evidence that vosoritide increases growth is now well established. Longer-term trial data show that children receiving the drug continue to grow faster than untreated children with achondroplasia over several years.

Parents may hope that treatment will also reduce some of the medical complications associated with achondroplasia, such as spinal stenosis, where narrowing of the spinal canal can put pressure on nerves, or improve independence later in life.

There is some encouraging early evidence. A 2026 trial found preliminary signs that early vosoritide treatment may improve spinal development. Another study found lower rates of some complications among children in vosoritide trials compared with published data about people who had not received the drug.
These findings are promising, but they do not yet establish whether treatment will prevent serious complications throughout life.

The spinal study followed children for only one year and included relatively small numbers, particularly when participants were divided into different age groups. Small studies make it harder to determine whether differences represent genuine treatment effects, especially for uncommon complications.

The second study included 230 children who received vosoritide, but compared their outcomes with previously published data rather than randomly assigning children to treated and untreated groups. Differences between these populations may have influenced the results.

There are also reasons for caution about assuming that starting treatment very early will prevent serious complications. Two infants who began vosoritide within days of birth still developed progressive foramen magnum stenosis, a narrowing at the base of the skull that can compress the brainstem and spinal cord. Both required surgery.

A report involving two children cannot establish how commonly this happens or whether vosoritide altered their risk. However, it demonstrates that early treatment does not necessarily prevent these complications.
What does a better quality of life mean?
Improving quality of life is another potential benefit of treatment, although measuring it is complicated.

Research involving people with achondroplasia has found that they can experience difficulties relating to health and physical functioning, alongside social barriers associated with living in a world designed around average-height bodies.

If quality-of-life measures include difficulty accessing buildings or experiences of discrimination, these problems cannot automatically be solved by changing a child’s body. Treatment may help some children manage everyday activities, but accessible environments and reduced discrimination are also needed.

The experience of receiving treatment deserves attention too. Vosoritide requires daily injections throughout the growing years. Research with seven families of children aged two to four found that injections could involve fear, pain and distress, although experiences varied.

These questions are especially relevant given the history of treatments intended to increase height. Limb-lengthening surgery, for example, remains contentious. A 2026 systematic review found that it can produce substantial increases in limb length, but involves prolonged treatment and carries a high risk of complications.
Decisions about such interventions have long raised questions about when children can meaningfully participate in choosing treatments that may affect them for years.
Who should decide what successful treatment looks like?

Adults with achondroplasia have been included in some research, and international guidance published in 2025 included two patient representatives. However, much of the evidence informing treatment decisions still comes from clinical trials and assessments made by clinicians and parents.

The guidance was financially supported by BioMarin, the manufacturer of vosoritide, and participants received honoraria for their involvement in the consensus process. The authors state that BioMarin did not influence the recommendations.

About 80% of people with achondroplasia are born to parents of average height. This makes the experiences of adults living with the condition particularly valuable when families are considering treatment.
Parents routinely make healthcare decisions for children who are too young to consent. They need clear information that distinguishes established benefits from hoped-for or still uncertain outcomes.

As children grow, their views should increasingly be included in decisions about their treatment. Current international guidance recommends that young people should have opportunities to agree to treatment, raise concerns or express disagreement. It also recommends that families are informed about the uncertainties surrounding long-term outcomes.

The ethical debate surrounding vosoritide therefore extends beyond whether the drug makes children taller. It also concerns which health benefits have been demonstrated, how treatment affects children day to day and who gets to define success.

Adults with achondroplasia have knowledge that clinical measurements cannot provide. Their experiences should help shape the outcomes researchers study and the information families receive when deciding whether treatment is right for their child.

articles.title: Early flu season: why you should get your jab sooner this year
articles.author: Simon Clarke, Associate Professor in Cellular Microbiology, University of Reading
paras: Data from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) shows more flu activity in September than in the same month of the past four years. However, flu is still circulating at relatively low levels in the community. If cases continue to rise over the coming weeks, this would suggest the flu season is starting earlier than usual.
Flu infections usually begin to climb in October and peak in the coldest months, around January.

One of the main types circulating is H1N1, known as swine flu, which caused an epidemic in the UK in 2009-10 and killed 457 people. The H1N1 virus circulating now has undergone changes that make it different from the version targeted by this year’s vaccine. This raises questions about how well the vaccine will protect people against it.

Flu viruses change a little from year to year. These changes, known as antigenic drift, can make it harder for the immune system to recognise a virus from a previous infection or vaccination. They affect proteins on the virus’s surface that the immune system recognises, potentially making a vaccine less effective against a changed version.

Each year, scientists at the World Health Organization study which flu viruses are circulating and use this information to recommend which versions should be included in vaccines. They have to make these decisions months in advance, so manufacturers have time to produce enough doses. Sometimes the viruses that spread turn out to be different from those the vaccine was designed to target.
The UKHSA is monitoring the changed virus closely. There is not yet enough information to know whether it will spread widely, cause more serious illness or make this year’s vaccine less effective.
A drifted strain does not guarantee a bad season. The variant may not become the dominant type, and the changes may not be enough to weaken the vaccine.

Last winter offers some reassurance. A drifted strain emerged after the northern hemisphere vaccine had been finalised, yet the jab still proved effective. Despite an early start to the 2025-26 season, flu activity and death rates were lower than the year before.
In England alone, the vaccination programme is believed to have prevented about 100,000 hospital admissions and 7,000 deaths.
How to tell the flu from a cold
With flu circulating earlier than usual, it helps to know how it differs from a common cold – and why symptoms alone can’t always tell you which virus you have.

Flu, COVID and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) share many symptoms, including fever, cough, fatigue and body aches. Telling them apart by symptoms alone is nearly impossible – although some patterns offer clues.

COVID can bring a sudden loss of taste or smell and shortness of breath, with symptoms building over a few days. Flu tends to strike abruptly, with a rapid onset of high fever, severe aches, chills and headaches.
Anyone who can turn up to work and function with a cough and runny nose probably has a cold, not flu – though their colleagues are unlikely to thank them for spreading it.

A test can help identify which virus is causing an infection. An antigen test detects proteins from the virus, while a PCR test looks for the virus’s genetic material. Both usually involve taking a swab from the nose or throat.

At this time every year, the NHS starts its flu vaccination publicity campaign; some GP surgeries send out emails and text messages offering a free flu vaccine to those who are eligible. High street pharmacies also begin advertising private jabs for a small fee, usually around £20.

If you’re eligible for a free NHS vaccine, it can be booked online. If you need to buy it privately through a high street pharmacy, it can usually be booked in branch or via their website, although stocks often sell out quickly. However you get a vaccine, it takes about 14 days to build maximum protection.

No vaccine programme is a guarantee of protection. But with flu activity rising early, it makes sense to get vaccinated sooner rather than later, so that your defences are in place before infections peak rather than while an epidemic rages.
Simon Clarke receives funding from the British Heart Foundation and Defence Science & Technology Laboratory.

articles.title: Nicotine pouches, vaping or cigarettes: Which nicotine product is actually the least harmful?
articles.author: Emma Fenske, Assistant Professor of Medicine, Addiction Medicine, University of Colorado Anschutz; Oregon Health & Science University
paras: “Do you smoke cigarettes?” I asked my patient succinctly in a recent clinic appointment.
He matter-of-factly responded, “Not anymore, I use Zyn pouches now.”
As with any patient, I gauged his readiness – or reluctance, in some instances – to disrupt his use of nicotine.
I asked about his interest in trying nicotine replacement therapy, a medical treatment that provides low, controlled amounts of nicotine. Initially, his response caught me by surprise.
“Aren’t I already using nicotine replacement products?” he asked astutely.

I gathered my thoughts and explained that while nicotine pouches are indeed a form of nicotine replacement, there are important caveats. Actual nicotine replacement therapy products are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration to help people quit smoking. In contrast, I explained that Zyn and other nicotine pouches are commercial tobacco products that are regulated by the FDA but are not FDA-approved smoking cessation medications.

My patient was surprised, because he had not realized there was a difference, which is a common misunderstanding. This encounter proved pivotal in the direction I would take in my subsequent clinical encounters.
As an addiction medicine physician, I often talk with patients who use nicotine in various forms.
Understanding how these products differ and what we know about their relative risks can help people make more informed choices.
Doing away with good/bad thinking
One of the most important distinctions I make when I talk to patients is distinguishing between the harms caused by nicotine itself and the harms caused by the way it is delivered.
Combustible tobacco products such as cigarettes expose users to thousands of chemicals produced by burning tobacco, while newer products such as vapes deliver nicotine without combustion.

But the lack of combustion does not make the newer products inherently safe. Nicotine remains addictive, and studies have raised concerns about its cardiovascular effects, including changes in heart rate, blood pressure and underlying vascular function.
The long-term health effects of newer nicotine products – particularly nicotine pouches – are not yet well established.

As a result, discussions about which nicotine product is appropriate for a given person do not fall into categories of “good” or “bad.” Rather, they involve nuanced conversations with patients to help them reach their goals and reduce overall harm.

What’s more, the health implications of a nicotine product depend not only on what is in it, but also on who is using it, how they use it and what it replaces. Relative harms vary significantly when talking about a current tobacco smoker who switches to an e-cigarette compared with a nonsmoker who starts vaping. The same distinction matters for nicotine pouches: Their lower exposure to many toxic chemicals does not make them risk-free, particularly for adolescents and other nonsmokers who have not previously used nicotine.
In 1965, 42.4% of the U.S. population smoked. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 11.6%.

This dramatic decline did not happen because of a single intervention, but through decades of accumulating scientific evidence, public education campaigns, warning labels, restrictions on advertising, smoke-free policies, higher tobacco taxes and shifts in social norms. At the same time, the tobacco landscape has evolved, with noncombustible nicotine products such as e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches becoming increasingly prominent.

In the U.S., 6.5% of adults reported using e-cigarettes in 2023, while past-year nicotine pouch use rose from 3.4% in 2023 to 5.9% in 2024. This fast-growing trend makes it clear that the public is in need of a better understanding of the relative harms of nicotine products.
To be clear, the major source of cigarette-related harm is burning tobacco, not simply the presence of nicotine.
Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, many of which are toxic and carcinogenic, culminating in approximately 2.5 million cancer deaths per year worldwide.
Patients also often land in the hospital with complications related to tobacco use, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cardiovascular disease.
While nicotine itself is the reason for dependence, the toxic mixture generated by burning tobacco leaves is what makes cigarette smoking so extraordinarily harmful.
Nicotine products compared
So, where do vaping, heated tobacco – also known as “heat-not-burn products” – cigarettes and oral nicotine fall on the spectrum of safety?

Electronic cigarettes – or vapes – generally contain fewer and lower levels of many toxic chemicals compared with cigarette smoke. However, inhaled aerosols can still contain harmful substances such as propylene glycol, which is often found in certain medicines, cosmetics and food products. While propylene glycol is classified as “generally safe” by the FDA for use in food, that designation does not establish that it is safe to inhale. The lungs process substances differently from the digestive system, and the health effects of chronic inhalation of propylene glycol through e-cigarette aerosol remain incompletely understood.

Heated tobacco products such as processed tobacco sticks, loose-leaf chambers, tobacco capsules and pods, or carbon-tipped pods typically heat tobacco to lower temperatures as opposed to burning it. This can lead to lower exposure to harmful substances compared with conventional cigarettes. However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers any tobacco product harmful, given that these products still deliver tobacco-derived nicotine and other toxins.

An increasingly prominent product is the nicotine pouch, such as the brand-name product Zyn. Sales of nicotine pouches in the U.S. have increased substantially in recent years, particularly since 2023. Unlike traditional smokeless tobacco, nicotine pouches contain no tobacco leaf; instead, they contain nicotine, flavorings and other ingredients. Users typically place a pouch between the upper lip and gum, where nicotine is absorbed through the tissues of the mouth.

Nicotine pouches generally result in lower exposure to many toxic substances, given that there is no combustion or inhaled aerosols. However, they can deliver substantial amounts of nicotine. Depending on the product, a single pouch may contain several milligrams of nicotine – comparable to or exceeding the amount of nicotine you would otherwise get from a cigarette. These products therefore remain addictive.
With all nicotine products, the relevant comparison is not “safe” versus “dangerous,” but rather “more harmful” versus “less harmful.
FDA-approved nicotine replacement therapy

Nicotine replacement therapy, on the other hand, is an FDA-approved medical treatment that delivers controlled, low amounts of nicotine without the many carcinogens and toxic chemicals found in tobacco smoke. These products come in the form of patches, gum, lozenges, nasal sprays and inhalers, intended to reduce cravings and withdrawal while helping people gradually move away from tobacco use.

Unlike nicotine replacement therapies, which are FDA-approved and supported by strong evidence of effectiveness for smoking cessation, e-cigarettes are not FDA-approved cessation treatments, despite evidence that they can help some people quit smoking. Evidence for nicotine pouches as a cessation aid remains limited, and they have not been FDA-approved for this purpose.
Patterns of nicotine and tobacco use also vary considerably across countries and populations, reflecting differences in culture, tobacco-control policies, product availability and patterns of use.

Similarly, access to smoking-cessation treatment and harm-reduction resources varies substantially from country to country. In the U.K., for example, cessation services are integrated into the country’s National Health Service, while Australia provides state-based "Quit” line services and permits regulated access to some nicotine vaping products through pharmacies. Many countries have limited or no comprehensive services focused on smoking cessation, and access to medications such as nicotine replacement therapy remains uneven.
Putting nicotine risk in perspective

For people who do not use nicotine, there is little reason to start. For people who smoke, quitting remains the best option. But if quitting is not immediately achievable, moving away from combustible tobacco may reduce exposure to harmful chemicals in cigarette smoke.

The goal is not to label every nicotine product “good” or “bad,” but to help people understand the trade-offs – and to make choices that move them toward less harm and, ultimately, away from nicotine dependence.

articles.title: That brightly packaged sexual enhancement pill at the gas station might be laced with dangerous drugs
articles.author: Andrew Yockey, Assistant Professor of Health and Kinesiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
paras: Brightly colored packaging, promises of better sexual performance and names like “Rhino,” “Anaconda” and “Magnum” make sexual enhancement products difficult to miss. They can be found online, in convenience stores and at gas stations, and some can even be ordered through delivery services.
But what’s inside the package may be considerably different from what appears on the label.

In May 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration warned consumers not to use a sexual enhancement product called Rhino 7S Type F3 7000, one of many Rhino-branded products. Laboratory testing had found that it contained two ingredients that did not appear on its label: sildenafil – the active ingredient in the prescription erectile dysfunction medication Viagra – and acetaminophen, the widely used pain reliever also sold as Tylenol.
This finding was not an isolated incident.
Dating back to 2007, the FDA has maintained an expanding list of health fraud scams, including sexual enhancement and energy products found to contain hidden pharmaceutical ingredients.

Today, the sexual enhancement market is still going strong – and still putting out adulterated substances. Seven new products were added to the FDA’s list in September 2026. Recent warnings have involved pills, gummies, honey products, coffee and even chocolates marketed as sexual enhancers.

As a public health researcher who studies substance use and health behaviors with unregulated products, I see these products as part of a larger challenge created by global supply chains, online commerce and a regulatory system that struggles to keep pace with rapidly changing products.
Supplements are regulated – but not like prescription drugs

In the U.S., the FDA regulates dietary supplements under a different framework than for prescription and over-the-counter drugs. Those drugs undergo a rigorous application process involving three phases of trials that usually take nearly a decade to complete.

Supplements, on the other hand, are regulated under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, which holds manufacturers responsible for ensuring that their supplements are safe and properly labeled. So dietary supplements aren’t completely unregulated, but they generally do not go through the FDA’s premarket approval process. This means the FDA does not approve them for safety and effectiveness before they reach consumers, as it does with medications.

That creates an important distinction between pharmaceutical drugs like Viagra and products marketed as dietary supplements, such as many Rhino-branded sexual enhancement products. Viagra is an FDA-approved prescription drug: Its active ingredient, sildenafil, has been evaluated in clinical trials for safety, effectiveness, dosing and manufacturing quality for an approved medical use.

After a dietary supplement goes to market, the FDA periodically inspects its manufacturing facilities and collects and tests some products. But it does not routinely test every supplement on store shelves. Instead, the agency prioritizes products associated with illnesses or injuries and those suspected of containing fraudulent, adulterated or otherwise illegal ingredients.
Hidden Viagra – and much more

Sildenafil and tadalafil, the active ingredients in Viagra and Cialis, belong to a class of medications called phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors. They are effective treatments for erectile dysfunction when appropriately prescribed.

But consuming these drugs unknowingly is very different from taking them under medical supervision. They are known to interact with nitrate medications, including nitroglycerin used by some people with heart disease. The combination can produce a dangerous drop in blood pressure.

The Rhino 7S case presented an additional risk: undeclared acetaminophen. It was not clear why acetaminophen was present in the supplement or how it got there. Someone taking the supplement while also using Tylenol, cold medicine or other acetaminophen-containing products could unknowingly exceed recommended amounts. Acetaminophen overdose can cause severe liver injury and, in extreme cases, acute liver failure or death.

Research suggests that adulteration is not limited to a handful of recognizable drug ingredients. A 2023 scientific review identified 112 unapproved phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors and related compounds that had been detected as adulterants in sexual enhancement products between 2003 and mid-2023. Adulterated supplements can contain approved drugs, unapproved analogues and other modified compounds.
This is not solely an American problem. Studies have identified undeclared erectile dysfunction drugs in supplements sold in Europe, Asia, the Middle East and elsewhere.

In one study of 158 sexual enhancement supplements available in the United Arab Emirates, researchers found undeclared sildenafil, tadalafil or vardenafil in more than 12% of all sexual enhancement products they tested.

The World Health Organization has warned that increasingly complex international supply chains and the growth of e-commerce make controlling substandard and falsified health products particularly difficult. The makers of these products might source their ingredients from one country, manufacture or package them in another and sell them online to a consumer thousands of miles away.

Illicit international pharmaceutical commerce is a major problem worldwide. From December 2024 to May 2025, the international law enforcement body Interpol conducted Operation Pangea XVII, in which authorities in 90 countries seized more than 50 million doses of illicit pharmaceuticals. Erectile dysfunction medications were the second-most commonly seized product type, behind psychostimulants, which are drugs that affect how the brain regulates dopamine.

The following year, another international law enforcement operation disrupted roughly 13,000 websites, social media pages and channels and automated bots connected to illicit medicine sales. Erectile dysfunction medications were again among the most frequently seized products.

But identifying one dangerous product does not eliminate the broader market. Packaging can change. Products can disappear and reappear under new names. Sellers can move from one website or social media account to another. Manufacturers can also alter chemical ingredients.

Researchers who tracked a sexual enhancement supplement marketed as “POWER” from 2007 through 2022 found phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors in every version they tested, but the specific adulterants changed over time. Despite warnings and seizures by European food and health authorities, the product was still being sold online at the end of the study period.

Laboratory testing of supplements is therefore essential, but testing alone cannot solve the problem. Even the FDA acknowledges that its public warning list represents only a fraction of contaminated products being sold. In other words, a product’s absence from the FDA database should not be interpreted as evidence that it is safe.
Words such as “natural,” “herbal” or “dietary supplement” signal to consumers that a sexual enhancement product does not contain pharmaceutical ingredients. But that is not necessarily the case.

U.S. law requires a specific FDA disclaimer when supplement manufacturers make claims about function, but it does not require sexual enhancement supplements to carry a warning explaining that “natural” or “herbal” products may contain undeclared pharmaceutical ingredients. FDA labeling rules are therefore not designed to warn consumers specifically about hidden drugs in these products.

Online sales add another layer of complexity. Under federal law, some online marketplaces must verify identifying information from certain high-volume third-party sellers and provide consumers with a mechanism for reporting suspicious marketplace activity. But the law does not generally require marketplaces to test dietary supplements for hidden pharmaceutical ingredients or proactively report every potentially adulterated product to the FDA.

The appeal of these products is easy to understand: They offer a private, convenient and widely available solution to problems that many men find embarrassing to talk about. But that convenience can obscure a basic problem — consumers may have no reliable way to know whether the ingredients listed on the package match what is inside.

For sexual health products in particular, reducing that uncertainty will depend not only on regulation and surveillance, but also on making conversations about sexual health feel routine enough that people have safer places to turn for help.

articles.title: Chronic pelvic pain treatment should focus on quality of life, not pain alone
articles.author: Jasmine Hearn, Reader in Health Psychology, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: For many women living with chronic pelvic pain, finding an explanation for their symptoms can take years. Getting a diagnosis may bring some relief, but treatment does not always bring an end to the pain. Even when symptoms improve, their effects on sleep, work and everyday life can continue.

Chronic pelvic pain is persistent or recurring pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis. It can be linked to several conditions, including endometriosis, bladder pain syndrome and vulvodynia, which causes ongoing pain around the external genitals. Some women have more than one condition contributing to their symptoms.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows elsewhere in the body. It can cause painful periods, ongoing pelvic pain, fatigue and difficulties getting pregnant. Hormone treatments can reduce pain, while surgery can remove areas of endometriosis.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice), which produces treatment guidance for the NHS, recommends choosing endometriosis treatments according to someone’s symptoms and priorities, rather than how extensive the disease appears to be.

The amount of endometriosis visible does not always reflect the severity of someone’s pain. Some women with extensive disease experience relatively mild symptoms, while others have severe pain despite having little visible disease.

Across different causes of chronic pelvic pain, the nervous system can become more sensitive to pain signals over time, meaning discomfort may continue even after the original source has been treated. Muscles in the pelvic floor, which support organs including the bladder and bowel, can also become tense and contribute to pain.
Our recent study of 147 women with chronic pelvic pain – pain in the lower part of the abdomen lasting at least three months – examined how different treatments related to quality of life.

Nearly two-thirds of participants (91) reported endometriosis. Others reported conditions such as vulvodynia, bladder pain syndrome and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), previously known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a condition affecting hormones and periods.

Women who said they had undergone surgery for pelvic pain scored lower on a measure of physical quality of life covering areas such as sleep, mobility and everyday activities. Those who had used painkillers also reported poorer quality of life in several areas, including physical and emotional wellbeing.
These results do not mean the treatments made people worse. Women whose pain is more severe or difficult to treat may be more likely to undergo surgery or use painkillers.

The study asked women which treatments they had used at any point and how they were doing at the time of the survey. It cannot tell us whether those treatments helped, harmed or made no difference to a patient. Nor can it tell us how participants would have felt without them.

Surgery and hormone treatments remain important options for endometriosis. Nice guidance recommends discussing the benefits and risks of surgery, including the possibility that symptoms may return and further surgery may be needed.
But pain scores alone cannot tell us how well someone is living. Being able to sleep, work, exercise or spend time with family may be just as valuable to patients as a reduction in pain.
Looking beyond pain relief
In our study, only 31% of participants reported having used psychological therapies, such as counselling or structured treatments that help people manage distress.

Those who had received psychological support tended to report better emotional wellbeing and greater satisfaction with aspects of daily life. Because our study was a snapshot rather than a trial, we cannot conclude that therapy caused these improvements.
Psychological support can help people cope with disrupted sleep, strained relationships and the emotional toll of persistent pain. This does not suggest that their physical pain is imagined.

A review of seven trials involving 757 women with endometriosis found that psychological treatments may improve mental health and some pain symptoms, although weaknesses in the studies limit how certain we can be.

Pelvic health physiotherapy was also mentioned relatively rarely in our survey. However, because participants were not asked about it as a separate treatment category, we cannot reliably say how many had received it.

This specialist physiotherapy can help when muscles around the pelvis are tense or overactive. It may involve exercises, hands-on treatment and guidance on moving more comfortably. A review of 38 clinical trials found that approaches combining different forms of physical therapy reduced pain in some women with persistent pelvic pain.

These treatments can be used alongside medical care. A 2025 review found that care involving several types of healthcare professional could reduce pain more than treatment from a single speciality. However, the studies did not show a clear improvement in overall quality of life.

For women with endometriosis, effective care may therefore require surgery, medicines or hormone treatment alongside support for the wider effects of persistent pain. Which approaches are appropriate will depend on each person’s symptoms and circumstances.

Healthcare services need to assess more than whether pain has fallen on a numerical scale. Whether someone can sleep, manage work, maintain relationships and take part in everyday life should also help determine whether treatment is working.

This article draws on research undertaken by Darya Ghodosi, an MSc Health Psychology graduate from Manchester Metropolitan University, who led the study described here, under the supervision of Dr Jasmine Hearn.

articles.title: First case of teeth growing out of an eye socket – what you need to know about ‘ectopic teeth’
articles.author: Saroash Shahid, Reader in Dental Materials, Queen Mary University of London
paras: A 16-year-old boy in India has had a tooth removed from his left eye socket, between the eyelid and the eyebrow. He had noticed a painless swelling for about a month, but was only taken to hospital when two hard, whitish points began poking through. A scan revealed a fully formed canine tooth – an extremely unusual example of an ectopic tooth.

Ectopic teeth are teeth that develop or erupt in the wrong place. Instead of following the usual path to the mouth, they end up somewhere else. They can be normal baby or adult teeth, or sometimes extra teeth known as supernumerary teeth.

Ectopic teeth are most often found in the maxillary sinus – the hollow space behind the cheekbone – but they have also been found in the nasal cavity, palate, chin, jaw joint and eye socket. A review of 61 published cases found that they can go unnoticed for years or cause pain, swelling, headaches or difficulty opening the mouth. A tooth growing inside the nose can lead to a blocked nose, discharge and nosebleeds.
So how does a tooth end up somewhere as strange as an eye socket?

The face develops from several groups of cells and tissues that move and join together in the womb. Tooth development depends on interactions between some of these tissues. If this process goes awry, a tooth can sometimes develop in an abnormal location – even away from the mouth.

Developmental problems are not the only possible explanation. A review of ectopic teeth in the upper jaw also lists injuries, dental treatment and growths such as cysts and tumours as possible causes.

Having several extra teeth can sometimes be a sign of an inherited condition. One example is cleidocranial dysplasia, a rare genetic disorder that affects the development of bones and teeth. Other much rarer genetic conditions have also been linked to extra teeth.
The Indian teenager had no history of trauma, and doctors could not determine why teeth had developed in his eye socket.
How are ectopic teeth found and treated?

Whether an ectopic tooth needs removing depends on where it is and whether it is causing problems. An isolated tooth with no symptoms can sometimes just be monitored, but it may need to be removed if it causes an infection, blocks a passage, damages nearby structures or is linked to a cyst.
Doctors use scans to pinpoint the tooth and see what lies close to it. A CT scan can show whether it sits near the eyes, nerves or blood vessels, which helps them decide whether to operate.

Surgery ranges from a simple extraction to a complex operation. For teeth in the nose or sinuses, surgeons can often use an endoscope – a thin tube with a camera and surgical instruments on the end – to remove them through the nostrils rather than making a larger cut. A review identified 27 published cases in which ectopic teeth in the nose or sinuses were removed this way.

Before surgery, the most common symptoms were nasal obstruction, discharge, facial pain and nosebleeds. The review found that endoscopic removal worked in the reported cases, although the evidence comes from a handful of published cases rather than large clinical trials.

Removing an ectopic tooth does not mean another ordinary tooth will grow in its place. But people with one supernumerary tooth can sometimes have others, so doctors may use scans to look for them. A few reports describe another extra tooth developing in the same area after removal, although this appears to be extremely rare.
In the Indian teenager’s case, the scan found no other ectopic teeth. His tooth had simply ended up in a very unusual place.

articles.title: Can NAD+ supplements help us age more healthily? Here’s what the science shows
articles.author: Justin Roberts, Professor of Nutritional Physiology, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: Anti-ageing supplements are everywhere, from advertising campaigns to social media feeds. Promising everything from increased energy to a longer life, they come in many forms, from powders containing multiple ingredients to single-nutrient capsules.
One molecule in particular, NAD+, has attracted growing interest, with claims it can boost energy, improve vitality, slow ageing and even help us live longer.
But does the science support these claims? And can NAD+ supplements really help us age more healthily?

NAD+ (short for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is found in every cell in our bodies. It plays an essential role in helping our cells turn food into energy. Without it, many of the processes that keep us alive would be unable to function.

NAD+ also supports numerous enzymes and proteins, including sirtuins, which help regulate inflammation, DNA repair and the function of mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy our cells need.

Research suggests that NAD+ levels decline as we get older. This is partly because damage to our DNA accumulates over time, activating enzymes that use up NAD+ more quickly. Another enzyme, called CD38, also becomes more active with age and inflammation, increasing NAD+ use. Meanwhile, our cells may become less efficient at producing it.
The extent of this decline varies between people and different tissues, with some studies suggesting that NAD+ levels may fall by between 10% and 80% as we age.
Lower NAD+ levels have been linked to reduced energy production in cells, slower DNA repair and other changes associated with ageing.

Animal studies suggest that increasing NAD+ levels may improve muscle function and metabolism and even cognitive function, encouraging researchers to investigate whether similar benefits are possible in humans.
Can supplements boost our NAD+ levels?

There is limited evidence that taking NAD+ itself as a supplement effectively increases NAD+ levels, as it is broken down during digestion. A potential solution to this could be liposomal NAD+, where the molecule is enclosed in tiny fat-based structures designed to improve absorption.

A 2026 study involving 14 people found that taking 1,000mg of liposomal NAD+ daily for two weeks increased NAD+ levels inside cells by more than 64%. However, larger, carefully controlled studies are needed to confirm this finding.

Most human research has instead focused on NAD+ precursors: substances the body uses to make NAD+. These include two compounds derived from vitamin B3, nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
There is good evidence that both can increase NAD+ levels in the blood.

In one randomised, placebo-controlled study involving 140 overweight but otherwise healthy adults aged 40–60, NR supplementation increased blood NAD+ levels over eight weeks. The greatest increase occurred among those taking 1,000 mg (milligrams) daily, whose levels rose by 142% after two weeks and remained elevated throughout the study.

Another study involving 30 healthy adults found that taking 250 mg of NMN daily increased blood NAD+ levels by around 50% after four weeks, with levels remaining elevated throughout the 12-week trial.
High doses of vitamin B3 may also increase NAD+, although these can be poorly tolerated over longer periods.

Together, these findings suggest that NAD+ precursors can successfully raise blood NAD+ levels. However, whether this also increases levels in other tissues, such as muscles and organs, remains unclear.
Can increasing NAD+ levels help us age more healthily?

Animal studies have produced encouraging results, with NAD+ precursors improving physical performance, insulin sensitivity and the way cells produce energy. One study found that giving older mice NR for six weeks increased their lifespan by an average of 39 days, equivalent to around 5%.
However, results from human studies have been less convincing.
A recent systematic review examined 33 human studies and found inconsistent effects on physical function, metabolism and other measures of healthy ageing.

For example, one study involving men aged over 65 found that taking 250 mg of NMN daily for 12 weeks improved walking speed by around 7% and left-hand grip strength by approximately 4%. Both are useful measures of physical function as we age. However, only 20 of the 42 participants completed the full study as planned, so larger trials are needed to confirm these findings.
In contrast, a 24-week study involving 14 older men with diabetes and reduced physical function found no significant improvements in walking speed or grip strength after taking the same dose of NMN.
These differences highlight how difficult it is to draw firm conclusions from small studies involving people with different health conditions.

There have been some other promising findings. A study involving recreational runners found that taking 600 mg or 1,200 mg of NMN daily alongside exercise training for six weeks improved some measures of the body’s ability to use oxygen during exercise.

This raises the possibility that NAD+ precursors could improve certain aspects of exercise performance. However, further research is needed to establish whether these effects lead to longer-term improvements in fitness or healthier ageing.
NAD+ supplements: should you take them?
The growing research into NAD+ supplements is certainly intriguing. There is good evidence that precursors such as NR and NMN can increase blood NAD+ levels.
However, we still lack convincing evidence that these supplements can help us stay healthier for longer, reduce age-related decline or extend our lives.
Larger, longer clinical trials are needed to establish whether these supplements can lead to meaningful health benefits influencing our healthspan or lifespan.

For now, if you want to age healthily, the strongest evidence continues to support eating a varied, nourishing diet, managing stress and taking regular physical activity that helps maintain strength, fitness and mobility as you get older.

articles.title: Cottage cheese, sunscreen and pimple popping: Strange Health is back for season two
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: What do cottage cheese, sunscreen and pimple popping have in common?

They are all heading our way in the new series of Strange Health, the podcast from The Conversation that investigates the odd, awkward and occasionally disgusting questions raised by our bodies and the health trends surrounding them.
We’re back for season two, with a new batch of questions that have been bothering us, fascinating us or sending us down unexpectedly strange research rabbit holes.
If you missed the first series, Strange Health takes the things people are talking about, searching for and sometimes doing to themselves, then asks researchers what the science actually says.

This time, we’ll be looking at cottage cheese, which seems to have escaped from the back of the fridge and become one of the internet’s favourite foods … cottage cheese brownies, anyone? We’ll also investigate some of the alarming claims circulating about sunscreen. Do sunscreens really contain cancer-causing toxins? And if you’re worried about what is in a bottle from the chemist, is making your own sun cream at home a sensible alternative?

Dermatologists have spent years telling us that squeezing spots is a terrible idea. It can damage the skin, increase inflammation and potentially leave scars. So why do videos showing people doing exactly that attract audiences of millions?

I would particularly like an answer to this one because, despite knowing perfectly well that it’s probably not the best use of my time, I am among that enormous audience. There is something horrifyingly compelling about a good pimple-popping video, and season two will try to work out why.
We’re also returning with a little extra spring in our step because Strange Health recently won best health and wellbeing podcast at the Publisher Podcast Awards 2026.
We were delighted, especially because the award suggests plenty of other people share our appetite for exploring the stranger corners of health and medicine.
And now we want your help.

What have you always wanted to know about your body? Which health claim have you seen online and thought, surely that can’t be right? Is there a habit, symptom or trend you would love somebody to investigate properly?

articles.title: I teach doctors how to interpret test results – and the labels ‘normal’ and ‘abnormal’ often hide what matters most
articles.author: Amiran Baduashvili, Associate Professor of Medicine, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: Mr. V felt tightness across his chest. His deepest breaths felt shallow. He sought help at an emergency department, where a resident physician found several worrying signs, including swelling of his hands and legs as well as heart enlargement on a chest X-ray.
Everything seemed to point to one diagnosis: heart failure, where the heart’s inability to pump blood efficiently causes fluid to build up in the body. But one result did not fit.

To diagnose heart failure, doctors often check blood levels of a hormone called BNP, which the heart releases under strain. Mr. V’s BNP levels came back normal. The resident remembered learning that BNP can be falsely normal in patients with obesity or who are overweight, even when they have heart failure. With that in mind, he dismissed the normal BNP result and ordered a diuretic to help Mr. V shed excess fluid – standard treatment for heart failure.

But Mr. V did not feel any better. The next day, a colleague of mine who was supervising the medical team examined him with an ultrasound and made a diagnosis that had been overlooked: cardiac tamponade, a life-threatening condition in which a build-up of fluid in the sac surrounding the heart compresses it so tightly that it can barely pump.

A squeezed heart needs more blood running through it, not less, so the diuretic could have been fatal. Luckily, his heart held on long enough for doctors to rush him to an operating room and drain the fluid, saving his life. Could this close call have been avoided?
The resident was right: Many patients with heart failure and excess body fat do have normal BNP levels. However, “normal” is not as simple as it sounds.

Doctors generally consider BNP values under 100 picograms per milliliter, or pg/mL, to be normal. Patients with excess weight and heart failure often have a BNP below 100, but usually not by much. A BNP value under 50 is uncommon in heart failure, even in very overweight patients. Mr. V’s BNP was 14.

This result was not just normal. It was so low that it argued strongly against a diagnosis of heart failure. But the label “normal” treated a BNP of 14 the same as a BNP of 95, hiding the very information that could have prompted doctors to look for another explanation for Mr. V’s symptoms.

Mr. V’s case reveals a deeper flaw in how doctors are trained to interpret lab results. Buried inside the word “normal” is key information that tells doctors how strongly a test result argues against a diagnosis. Some normal results can make a diagnosis slightly less likely, while others may effectively rule it out.

As a physician who studies and teaches how best to interpret diagnostic tests, I often wonder: If a test result carries so much nuanced information, why do some doctors settle for a simple “normal” or “abnormal” reading instead?
When ‘normal’ isn’t normal

The 21st Century Cures Act, signed into law by President Barack Obama in 2016, gave patients greater access to their own healthcare information. Through online portals, people can often view their test results before a clinician has the chance to review them.

Those results usually come paired with a simple cutoff separating “normal” from “abnormal.” Although there are benefits to transparency, there is also a hidden cost: false alarm from “abnormal” results, and false reassurance from “normal” ones.

When I teach clinicians how to interpret diagnostic results, many are surprised to learn that, for numerous tests, mildly abnormal results may lower the likelihood of the disease they’re used to diagnose.

Take D-dimer, a blood test that doctors often order to determine whether patients with chest pain or difficulty breathing have a blood clot. A D-dimer above 500 nanograms per milliliter, or ng/mL, is labeled abnormal. But values between 500 and 1,000 actually slightly decrease the odds of a blood clot. For those at low risk for blood clots, a result in that range is nearly as reassuring as a “normal” one, even though it’s flagged as abnormal on the report. The reverse can also be true.

Cholesterol is another example. Laboratories consider levels of LDL, or “bad” cholesterol, under 100 milligrams per deciliter, or mg/dL, to be normal. However, for patients who have already suffered a heart attack or stroke, anything above 55 is too high.

Sorting results into normal and abnormal categories has a certain appeal. It makes interpreting tests easy and fast. It also reduces uncertainty. However, human biology is far from simple, and a lot of nuances are lost in that simplification.

The exact value of a test result tells doctors far more than the mere labels “normal” or “abnormal” can. Imagine a blood pressure machine that simply gave a reading of “elevated” or a heart rate monitor that read “low” instead of specific numbers. Doctors would never use such imprecise tools. Yet they often do when it comes to diagnostic tests.
Patients should feel empowered to ask their clinicians what a specific number means for them. A “normal” or “abnormal” label is a starting point for a conversation, not the final word.

My colleagues and I conducted a study that asked a simple question: What if, alongside each lab value, doctors saw not just a cutoff value for normal, but also how strongly each value points toward – or away from – a diagnosis?
We call this metric an interval likelihood ratio. It tells doctors how much a test result should raise or lower the odds that a patient has a specific diagnosis.

To derive these ratios, researchers run a test in many patients with and without the diagnosis the test is designed to pick up. Rather than drawing a single line between “normal” and “abnormal,” researchers divide the results into ranges. Each range compares how often patients with or without the diagnosis had a result within those values.

To test whether interval likelihood ratios help improve medical decisions, we recruited more than 600 clinicians across four major U.S. academic institutions. Each participant was asked to read two scenarios like Mr. V’s and make a key decision on how to manage a patient’s case based on a lab result. Everyone saw the exact test value. We randomly assigned some participants to see the numerical lab value alongside the standard cutoff for a normal result, and others to see it alongside interval likelihood ratios.
The difference between how these groups performed was not trivial.

Clinicians assigned to see interval likelihood ratios made a correct call 93 out of 100 times, while those seeing a single cutoff got it right 82 times out of 100. In other words, for roughly 1 in 10 patients like Mr. V, doctors could make a better decision if shown the degree to which a test result changes the odds of a particular diagnosis compared to merely seeing a cutoff for the normal range.
Improving how test results are displayed could help patients make better sense of their own results, help clinicians avoid critical mistakes and help health systems deliver safer care.
Clinicians learn to understand the degree to which a particular test result is abnormal through experience, shaping their intuition as they review new test results. However, intuition can be wrong.

Diagnostic errors remain one of the leading causes of harm in medicine. Our study found that interval likelihood ratios helped attending physicians, residents and advanced practice providers make better decisions, regardless of how long they’ve been practicing or their training background.

There is a legal dimension to how test results are labeled. A result flagged “abnormal” can feel like it obligates a clinician to act, such as ordering another scan, even when their own judgment says otherwise. Interval likelihood ratios can change that calculus, providing clinicians a documented, evidence-based reason to hold off ordering advanced tests and potentially saving their patients from the health risks they may entail.

The challenge is how and where to find high-quality research studies to derive interval likelihood ratios when electronic health records display only binary cutoffs as aids to interpreting test result values. It is also important to note that our study showed clinicians made better decisions in simulated scenarios, which is not the same as making decisions with real patients. The next step is testing whether these gains hold up in everyday practice, across different institutions, care settings and lab tests.
Test results are more than normal or abnormal. For patients like Mr. V, the difference between these labels and the numbers behind them can be the difference between life and death.
Amiran Baduashvili is the founder of EBM Clarity, Inc, which owns an online course in diagnostic reasoning. His earns no income from this endeavor.

articles.title: Escape rooms give healthcare students a safe place to get things wrong
articles.author: Rhi Carter, Lecturer in Occupational Therapy, University of Winchester
paras: The buzzer goes off. Three occupational therapy students are convinced they have worked out what should happen to their patient next. They are wrong.

Nobody is harmed, and no real patient is waiting. The escape room gives students a safe place to practise something healthcare professionals do every day: using their knowledge to make decisions when information is incomplete, situations change and the answer is not obvious. Getting it wrong and trying again is part of the learning.

Healthcare education has a challenge. Students can learn anatomy and physiology, theory and professional standards, but eventually they must use that knowledge with a real person. Real people rarely behave like case studies.

Healthcare can be fast-moving and pressured. Information changes, priorities compete and professionals may have to make decisions without everything they would like to know. The person at the centre may also have different priorities from those the professional expected.

Healthcare professionals therefore need more than knowledge. They need to apply it, adapt it and sometimes rethink it as a situation develops. The Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) standards for occupational therapists, for example, require practitioners to use professional judgement, analyse information, solve problems and make reasoned decisions.
So how can students practise that before their decisions affect somebody for real?

I designed an escape room for occupational therapy students to explore that question. Working in teams of three, students receive simulated emergency department notes and must decide what matters, make connections and agree what to do next. When they think they have the answer, they press the buzzer.

It sounds like a game because it is one. But making education playful does not automatically make it educational. The escape room provides the activity. What students are required to think about and discuss is what gives it educational value.

Escape rooms are already used across healthcare education. A systematic review of 52 studies found them being used with students in medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry and physiotherapy. Teamwork, experiential learning and discussion afterwards were important features, although evidence that escape rooms produce better learning than conventional teaching remained inconclusive.
In my escape room, the puzzles and buzzer create uncertainty, but students must talk to each other, explain their reasoning and sometimes change their minds.

Research into game-based approaches in healthcare education also suggests potential benefits. A systematic review of gamification found that some approaches improved students’ engagement with learning and sometimes their learning outcomes. However, many of the studies lacked strong comparison groups, so the authors called for more rigorous research.
The important question is therefore not simply whether an activity is enjoyable, but what the game asks students to learn.

When I designed the escape room, I did not start with the puzzles. I started with what the students already knew, what I wanted them to learn and what I wanted them to do with that knowledge. If I only wanted to test whether they could remember facts, I could put multiple-choice questions behind padlocks and call it an escape room.

Instead, uncertainty is built into the experience. Students are not immediately told which information matters. One person may notice something another has dismissed, so they have to listen to different interpretations and reach a decision together.

Sometimes they move forward. Sometimes the buzzer tells them their reasoning has taken them in the wrong direction. It introduces pressure without the consequences of making the wrong decision in real healthcare.
The discussion after the game
The learning does not finish when students escape. Afterwards, they discuss why they made particular decisions, what they overlooked and whether somebody else’s perspective changed their thinking.

That stage is important. A review of clinical reasoning games found that games could give healthcare students opportunities to consider a patient’s situation, gather information and decide what to do. But reflection was one of the parts of clinical reasoning least often incorporated into the games researchers examined.

The discussion afterwards therefore allows students to examine how they reached a decision rather than simply finding out whether it was right or wrong. Reflection is also part of the professional standards for occupational therapists, which require practitioners to reflect on and review their practice.

Learning through doing has particular relevance to occupational therapy. The profession is concerned with what people do and how occupation relates to ideas of doing, being, becoming and belonging. These concepts are used to understand people’s experiences of occupation and the place activities have in their lives.
There is therefore a useful parallel in asking students to learn through activity rather than only hearing or reading about practice.

This approach does not require virtual reality headsets or expensive simulation technology. My escape room uses simulated hospital notes, puzzles, a buzzer and a story, allowing it to be incorporated into an ordinary taught session. What changes is what students are asked to do with the information they are given.

An escape room cannot reproduce the pressure or complexity of making decisions about a real person. But it can let students experience uncertainty, make a mistake, reconsider their reasoning and try again.

Healthcare professionals will encounter situations no lecturer could write neatly into a case study. Preparing students for those moments means teaching them knowledge, but also giving them opportunities to practise what happens when the answer is not immediately clear.
